doc.title: Robert Glasper interviewed by Greg Thomas, Clinton, New York, February 20, 2016

title: Living in jazz, R&B, church and hip-hop worlds
summary: Greg Thomas raises genre; Glasper describes playing with Common, Q-Tip, Mos Def and the Roots, and says each genre has its own vibe.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: That’s very interesting. You saying this. Because to me it brings up the issue of genres.
Yup.
So for you, you grew up hearing all of this.
Um hum.

You were exposed to it, you were around it, you ended up playing it. So as I said to you back in September, when I listen to your music and I hear you and I see you going in © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-

these different areas, even when I frankly didn’t even know the extent of your musical associations with Bilal and this one and Mos Def. I didn’t really know that. But I was like this is organic. It wasn’t a trick. It wasn’t a marketing ploy.
Right.
Sometimes you can hear somebody and it doesn’t sound like it really came from their heart.
Right.
You know what I mean?
Yeah, totally.
But with you it was like, I was like, well yeah, I can hear that. The cat can play but he’s doing that, he’s doing this.
And with all my influences I actually live in those worlds musically.
Simultaneously.

Simultaneously. That’s why I can, that’s why I feel like I play them well, because I literally was on the road with the masters of their craft. You know what I mean? So like I say I played damn near my whole life in church, so that’s one part. But then when I got to New York pretty much as soon as I got to New York, you know, I was in the company of Common and Q-Tip and Mos Def and all those guys, and I started in the Roots. And Questlove used to call me to play with the Roots when I was in college a lot. Then after college I played with them a lot. So now I’m in the hip-hop world and I’m playing that. I’m watching James Poyser and I’m playing all these hip-hop tracks now and learning how to play that vibe. You know, that’s the vibe. I get it. Boom-boom-boom.
But each genre has a particular vibe.

Each genre has a particular vibe and it’s very egotistical — a lot of jazz musicians think because they have a lot of chops that every other music is easy to play and you can just do it. But that’s not the case.

Well T.S. Monk, Thelonious Monk’s son, who for years played in R&B, he made it very clear, he’s like, you know, you’re playing that? Can you keep that time right there? Can you keep it there? Can you keep it there like that?
Right. Bum-bum-be. Yeah. That’s T.S. That’s my cousin-in-law.
Oh yeah?
Yeah.
Oh okay. Small world.
Small world. So yeah, so basically I went through the training camp of each of those genres of music you know what I mean, basically. In a way.
So then that’s how in a way, you’re a producer.
Right. © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-
